items.ask: Define Pareto dominance when minimizing objectives f₁, …, f_k.
items.answer: Design a dominates design b when fᵢ(a) ≤ fᵢ(b) for every objective i and fⱼ(a) < fⱼ(b) for at least one objective j.
items.cue: At least as good everywhere, strictly better somewhere.

items.ask: State the Metropolis acceptance rule and cooling schedule used in simulated annealing.
items.answer: Accept a move with probability P = min(1, exp(−Δf/T)), Δf = f_new − f_current: every downhill move, and uphill moves with probability exp(−Δf/T). Cool geometrically, T_k = T₀αᵏ with 0 < α < 1.
items.cue: Annealed metal: hot atoms hop uphill freely, cold atoms settle into the deepest well.

items.ask: Give the ε-constraint method for a two-objective problem.
items.answer: Minimize f₁ subject to f₂ ≤ ε plus the original constraints. Sweep ε from the f₂ minimum to the f₂ value at the f₁ minimum; each solve gives one Pareto point, nonconvex parts included. The multiplier on f₂ ≤ ε is the local trade-off slope.
items.cue: Keep one objective, cap the other: lower the ε ceiling one notch at a time along the front.

items.ask: List the Nelder Mead moves in the order they are tested.
items.answer: Sort vertices, take the centroid of all but the worst, reflect the worst. Reflection beats the best: try expansion. Between best and second worst: accept. Worse than second worst: contract (outside if better than worst, else inside). Contraction fails: shrink toward the best.
items.cue: Reflect, Expand, Contract, Shrink: flip the worst point, stretch further, pull in, then huddle around the best.

items.ask: State the first-order and second-order conditions for convexity of a differentiable f on a convex set.
items.answer: First order: f(y) ≥ f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀ(y − x) for all x, y in the set. Second order: ∇²f(x) ⪰ 0 at every x in the set. A Hessian ∇²f ≻ 0 everywhere gives strict convexity.
items.cue: Tangent plane sits below the graph; curvature bends upward at every point of the domain.

items.ask: How does a change to log variables help with a drag function such as D = aV²S + c/(V²S)?
items.answer: In (V, S) the Hessian of D is indefinite where parasite drag exceeds induced drag, so D is nonconvex. With v = ln V and s = ln S each term becomes exp(affine), so D is convex in (v, s): geometric programming, where a local minimum is global.
items.cue: Logs turn products into sums; exponentials of straight lines always bend upward.

items.ask: Give the complex step derivative and its error order.
items.answer: f'(x) ≈ Im[f(x + ih)]/h with truncation error O(h²). It involves zero subtractive cancellation, so h can be as small as 10⁻²⁰ and the derivative is accurate to machine precision.
items.cue: Step sideways into the imaginary axis: the derivative arrives alone in the imaginary part, so tiny h keeps every digit.

items.ask: Contrast reduced space and full space (simultaneous analysis and design) formulations.
items.answer: Reduced space: the analysis solves R(x, u) = 0 at every design and the optimizer sees x alone. Full space: the states u join the variables and R(x, u) = 0 becomes equality constraints, met together with optimality at convergence.
items.cue: Nested dolls versus one big table: solve inside each call, or lay every state on the optimizer's table.

items.ask: How does IDF keep the disciplines consistent?
items.answer: IDF adds coupling targets as optimization variables, runs each discipline independently on those targets, and imposes consistency equality constraints, target = computed coupling output. The coupled system is consistent at the converged optimum, while intermediate designs may be inconsistent.
items.cue: Each discipline gets a copy of its inputs; equality constraints make the copies match the originals at the end.

items.ask: How many runs does a central composite design use for k factors?
items.answer: 2ᵏ factorial corners + 2k axial points + n_c centre points. For k = 2 with one centre point: 4 + 4 + 1 = 9 runs, enough for the 6 terms of a full quadratic.
items.cue: Corners for interactions, stars for curvature, centre for pure error.

items.ask: State the conditions satisfied by the exact solution p* of the trust region subproblem.
items.answer: (B + λI)p* = −g, λ ≥ 0, λ(Δ − ‖p*‖) = 0, and B + λI positive semidefinite. λ = 0 gives the Newton step inside the region; λ > 0 puts p* on the boundary ‖p*‖ = Δ.
items.cue: Shift B by λ until the step fits the ball: these are the KKT conditions with ½‖p‖² ≤ ½Δ².

items.ask: Write the trust region subproblem.
items.answer: min over p of m(p) = f(x) + ∇f(x)ᵀp + ½pᵀBp subject to ‖p‖ ≤ Δ, with B the Hessian or a quasi-Newton approximation of it.
items.cue: A second-order Taylor model, trusted inside a ball of radius Δ.

items.ask: As λ grows from 0 toward infinity, how does p(λ) = −(B + λI)⁻¹g change for B ≻ 0?
items.answer: Its length falls steadily from the Newton step length ‖p_N‖ toward zero, and its direction turns from the Newton direction toward steepest descent −g.
items.cue: Huge λ swamps B: (λI)⁻¹ gives −g/λ, a short steepest descent step.

items.ask: Give the SQP step system for min f s.t. h(x) = 0.
items.answer: [[W, Aᵀ],[A, 0]][p; λ] = [−∇f; −h], with W = ∇²L the Lagrangian Hessian, A = ∇hᵀ the constraint Jacobian and λ the new multiplier. It is Newton's method on the KKT conditions.
items.cue: Newton on ∇L = 0 and h = 0: Hessian top left, Jacobian on the border, zeros in the corner.

items.ask: Describe the active set loop for an inequality constrained QP.
items.answer: Hold a working set of constraints as equalities and solve that equality QP. If the step violates a constraint, add it. If a working constraint has μ < 0, drop it. Stop when the step is feasible and every working μ ≥ 0.
items.cue: Add what blocks, drop what pulls the wrong way, stop when every wall pushes back.

items.ask: Give the augmented Lagrangian for h(x) = 0 and its multiplier update.
items.answer: L_A = f + λᵀh + (ρ/2)‖h‖². Minimize over x for fixed λ and ρ, then update λ ← λ + ρh(x). It converges at a finite ρ, which keeps each subproblem well conditioned.
items.cue: Lagrangian plus penalty: the penalty pushes early, and the multiplier update learns the exact constraint force.

items.ask: Give the minimum norm surrogate weights in summation form for n < m.
items.answer: Solve Σₖ(Σⱼφⱼ(xᵢ)φⱼ(xₖ))aₖ = yᵢ for i = 1, …, n, then wⱼ = Σᵢaᵢφⱼ(xᵢ). In vector form (ΦΦᵀ)a = y and w = Φᵀa.
items.cue: The weights live in the row space of Φ: build w from the sample rows of basis values.

items.ask: Give the matrix sizes when ridge regression is solved in primal and dual form, for n samples and m basis functions.
items.answer: Primal: (ΦᵀΦ + λI)w = Φᵀy, an m × m system. Dual: (ΦΦᵀ + λI)a = y, an n × n system, then w = Φᵀa. Both give the same w, so solve the smaller system.
items.cue: Push through identity: (ΦᵀΦ + λI)⁻¹Φᵀ = Φᵀ(ΦΦᵀ + λI)⁻¹. ΦᵀΦ is m × m, ΦΦᵀ is n × n.

items.ask: Define the ridge parameter λ and how it is chosen.
items.answer: λ ≥ 0 weights ‖w‖² against the squared error in min ‖y − Φw‖² + λ‖w‖². Larger λ shrinks the weights and smooths the fit; λ → 0 recovers least squares or the minimum norm fit. Choose λ by cross-validation.
items.cue: A dial from wiggly to smooth, set by the cross-validation error.

items.ask: State the second-order sufficient condition at a KKT point.
items.answer: zᵀ∇²L(x*)z > 0 for every z ≠ 0 tangent to the active constraints (∇hᵀz = 0 and ∇gᵢᵀz = 0 for active gᵢ with μᵢ > 0). Positive Lagrangian curvature on that tangent space gives a strict local minimum.
items.cue: Check curvature along the directions the constraints allow: the reduced Hessian is positive definite.

items.ask: What does complementary slackness say about each inequality constraint gᵢ ≤ 0?
items.answer: μᵢgᵢ(x*) = 0: an active constraint (gᵢ = 0) has μᵢ ≥ 0, and an inactive constraint (gᵢ < 0) has μᵢ = 0.
items.cue: A wall pushes back only when you lean on it.

items.ask: Write the BFGS update of the Hessian approximation B.
items.answer: B₊ = B − (Bs sᵀB)/(sᵀBs) + (yyᵀ)/(yᵀs), with s = x₊ − x and y = ∇f₊ − ∇f. It satisfies the secant condition B₊s = y and stays positive definite when yᵀs > 0.
items.cue: Remove the old curvature along s, add the measured curvature y: then B₊s = y.

items.ask: Give the Fletcher-Reeves nonlinear CG direction update.
items.answer: p₊ = −g₊ + βp with β = (g₊ᵀg₊)/(gᵀg), starting from p₀ = −g₀.
items.cue: New steepest descent plus a memory of the old direction, weighted by the ratio of squared gradient sizes.

items.ask: How do the eigenvalues of H set the shape of the contours of f = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx with H ≻ 0?
items.answer: Contour axes lie along the eigenvectors through the critical point, with semi-axis lengths proportional to 1/√λᵢ, so the long axis follows the smallest eigenvalue. κ = λ_max/λ_min measures the elongation.
items.cue: Steep direction, tight contours: a large λ squeezes, a small λ stretches.

items.ask: Give the quadratic interpolation step used inside a line search.
items.answer: Fit q(α) to φ(0), φ'(0) and φ(α₀): α₁ = −φ'(0)α₀²/(2[φ(α₀) − φ(0) − φ'(0)α₀]), the vertex of that parabola.
items.cue: Three facts make a parabola: value and slope at zero, value at the trial step. Jump to its vertex.
